prompt: Fix an integer $k\ge2$; label indices $i,j$ range over $\{1,\ldots,k\}$. Which operation is permitted by a standard $k$-expression for clique-width?

answers.text: For $i\ne j$, add every missing edge between the current label-$i$ and label-$j$ vertices.
answers.explanation: A join acts uniformly on two distinct label classes. It adds edges and leaves existing edges in place.

answers.text: Delete an arbitrary existing edge while preserving all labels.
answers.explanation: Edge deletion is not a primitive operation of a clique-width expression.

answers.text: Identify any two vertices of the same label.
answers.explanation: Clique-width expressions build graphs without contracting vertices.

answers.text: Add just one chosen edge between two otherwise indistinguishable labelled vertices.
answers.explanation: A join treats entire label classes uniformly, not chosen individual vertices within them.

answers.text: Complement adjacency between two label classes in one primitive step.
answers.explanation: The join adds all missing edges; it does not toggle or remove existing edges.

answers.text: Relabel one chosen vertex in a label class while leaving the others unchanged.
answers.explanation: The relabelling operation changes every vertex carrying the source label.

answers.text: Create an arbitrary nonempty labelled graph as a single atomic expression.
answers.explanation: The atomic expressions create single labelled vertices.

answers.text: Apply a same-label join $\eta_{i,i}$ as a primitive operation.
answers.explanation: The standard definition requires distinct labels. Same-label joins belong to a modified convention.

answers.text: Give one vertex several simultaneous construction labels.
answers.explanation: In the standard definition every vertex carries exactly one label at each stage.

answers.text: Join only across the two operands of a union, using their origin as an extra test.
answers.explanation: A standard clique-width join sees current labels, not which union operand a vertex came from; that origin-sensitive primitive is NLC-style.

sources.title: Ganian et al. — Shrub-depth: Capturing Height of Dense Graphs, §§2–4
